comments.author: jacquesm
comments.text: I've owned 1x2cV, 3xDS/ID (one a donor car), 2x Xantia and 1 XM. All of them had something that very few modern cars have, which is that they were quirky but interesting, both technology wise and to drive. If you knew them well you could do just about anything with them. Anyway, about that hydraulic system: a friend of mine who lived in IJmuiden was improving his house. To do so he had bought a load of concrete tiles in Amsterdam on an impulse (really, really good deal). So he called me up and asked if I could come and help shift them to IJmuiden. When I got there there was this absolutely massive pile and I figured this is not going to end well. I had dropped the rears seat (which you could pull out fairly easily, but the back cushions stayed in place) so there was quite a bit of room and two tiles fit side by side. So we stacked them pretty much to the ceiling and miraculously, the car just kept on adjusting ride height and ever gave any sign that it couldn't handle the load. All of the tiles fit. Then we drove to IJmuiden. It all went well until we hit the overpass over the road between Amsterdam and Haarlem on A9. The car took a bit of a dive into the dip and then came back out and came back out further than it went in. And did it again. Before long it was bouncing like a ball with the rear (which was pretty heavy) coming off the ground. I lost some speed and finally got the car to sit by the side of the road, still bouncing. Engine off, let the whole thing come to rest, engine back on, everything fine. We drove the last bit really slow, just in case. So, that's what an undampened servo oscillation looks like in a hydraulic system. After unloading the backseat went back in and it was just like before. DE-70-72, whoever has it now, that car is as solid as they come (it is still registered, this was more than 20 years ago, the car is from 1968 and it has been off the road for a long time). The hydraulic computer sits behind the left front wheel well behind a separate shield and it is super complicated, if you have to fix it you better know what you're doing.

comments.author: Svip
comments.text: Generally goes unnoticed (though not unmentioned), but until after the Xantia, the suspension system also included the brakes and the steering (which would technically not be permitted under modern EU car standards); which meant a leak would eventually not just cause a loss of suspension, but also a loss of steering and braking. Why incorporate the braking and the suspension? The mechanical height regulator could "feel" how much fluid it needed to fill the suspension with, in order to obtain the desired ride height; which meant it "knew" how heavy the vehicle was loaded, and thus apply the brakes accordingly. This is why in a proper Citroën hydraulic car, the brake pedal feels "weird", in that it doesn't go far down (and quickly becomes hard to press) (the DS tried to make this less confusion by making the pedal a "mushroom" button instead); because the idea is that you should apply gentle braking, and the car will figure out the necessary amount of braking force required (unlike just hitting the pedal like in a normal car, which would result in an almost hard stop). Why the steering then? I think that's more of a convenience thing, mechanically speaking, as it was already there to provide a form of power steering; though it is funny feeling it getting pumped up (steering was always the last portion to receive fluid during the pumping). At least, as far as I can tell, it has little bearing on the suspension or braking. I know the SM and CX tried the DIRAVI steering, which completely made the steering one way (so you couldn't feel the road); though it was fun to see the steering wheel self-righting even when parked. Full disclosure: I own a 1974 Citroën DS 23 and a 1998 Citroën Xantia Activa V6.

comments.author: twotwotwo
comments.text: It is true soundness bugs have been found, and the Lean community spends effort on it. But this page doesn't convey the gap between one incorrect verification and successfully misleading mathematicians about what is true: there are multiple checkers and you need bugs in all of them, without the input looking implausible on informal review. (For example, a DeepMind researcher created a 'proof' that passed Lean and (a then-week-old version of) nanoda by exploiting a different bug in each. But if you fed that into a regular old LLM (or to a human expert, but I mention LLMs b/c they can be assigned to review even very large volumes of Lean code) it would immediately say "no, this isn't real math.") The increase in soundness bugs found this year is notable, because LLMs are good at finding ways to their assigned goals, and they found some funny ones. And , besides fixes for the specific bugs, it led to broader work on hardening and alternative and verified kernels: https://leodemoura.github.io/blog/2026-10-15-lean-now-ships-... So you have fewer avenues than at the start of the year to get a proof of False OK'd by one proof-checker kernel, and it's much much harder to get one through the gauntlet invoked by `lake check --paranoid`. (This is also interesting as a(nother) example of the difficulty of making truly correct software -- you'd hope for proof-checker kernels to be pretty high on the correctness scale but seems like we've found 16-32 soundness bugs in a bunch of these.)

comments.author: dwheeler
comments.text: I think this is misleading for the proof-checkers in systems where multiple provers must pass for the proof to be accepted. In the case of Metamath, yes, soundness bugs have been found in the original "metamath" proof verifier, written in C. But to be accepted into the main proof databases (set.mm and iset.mm), proofs must pass "5 independently-created verifiers in 5 different programming languages: metamath (a C verifier by Norm Megill), mmj2 (a Java verifier by Mel O'Cat and Mario Carneiro), smetamath-rs (a high-speed Rust verifier by Stefan O'Rear), checkmm (a C++ verifier by Eric Schmidt), and mmverify.py a Python verifier by Raph Levien)." - https://us.metamath.org/ To me, that's a key countermeasure to the problem.

comments.author: gr_norm
comments.text: The call for further high-assurance work is good, but let's not miss the forest for the trees: some of these have been around for decades, and all the soundness bugs they've ever had fit in a tweet! (Or close to it.) Comfortably more than good enough for 99.9% of software, especially considering you'd still need to exploit such a soundness bug in a way that hides a further issue in the program being verified.

comments.author: amelius
comments.text: Pardon my ignorance but why are these proof checkers so large? Can't they be bootstrapped from a very small set of rules, which are easy to check?

comments.author: andai
comments.text: There's a deeper problem — I'm assuming it doesn't apply in the case of the math proofs because the problem itself has already been formulated in symbolic terms, by humans — but I've had this problem where, an agent proved the correctness of an implementation (within reason), but it proved it against its own incorrect understanding of what needed to be done. So in one case, what it built ended up being the exact opposite of what needed to be done! I found it amusing in that case l, that even if it had supplied me with a formal proof of correctness, the proof would also have passed, and the implementation would still have been completely useless! Because the LLM's understanding of what it was supposed to be doing in the first place was wrong. Communication is hard!

comments.author: SideQuark
comments.text: Background: Sarah Wynn-Williams worked at law firm 2002-2005, joined the New Zealand diplomatic service as a policy adviser 2007-2011, managing government relations at it's embassy in DC. She joined Meta in 2011, was in 2017, signed a standard severance agreement with a non-disparagement clause and an arbitration provision, and received $780,000 severance. She did not have to sign it, but signed it to get the money. It's a legal contract. She's been a high powered lawyer and well enough connected it's not at all likely she knew what she was signing. Especially since after being in her position for 6 years at Meta she likely oversaw many similar such events from the Meta side. In 2024, she filed a SEC complaint. In 2025 she publishes her book, Meta secures an emergency ruling from an American Arbitration Association arbitrator invoking her signed severance contract, she testifies to Congress. In 2026 she sued Meta Meta in federal court in the Northern District of California to vacate the arbitration, and U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín denies Wynn-Williams’s request to halt the arbitration. To head off more conjectures, the American Arbitration Association is well respected, and has massive experience representing both sides of such things. The Judge, a female, has been a long time fighter for social justice, was nominated by Biden, also very well respected. Given that the two seemingly best respected arbiters of these types of claims, who have both certainly seen both sides complaints, and given Sarah is a well connected, legally savvy person, I find it hard to believe the story is as one sided bad behavior as she claims.

comments.author: KaiserPro
comments.text: One of the things that may not be apparent from outside facebook is how the contracts work. Virtually everyone is on the same employment contract. The only thing that really changes is the name, wages and in some cases country specific addendums. The same goes for when you are fired. Everyone is given an NDA to sign when they yeet you. It offers you a choice: 1) sign it and Here is a large amount of cash (usually somewhere between 3 and 12 months wage) some health insurance, and a pathetic job search subscription. 2) don't sign it and get nothing You then are allocated 30 minutes with a lawyer, who tells you the choice is yours: take the money and sign the NDA, and never tell anyone of its existence. Or leave with nothing. The NDA is wonderfully comprehensive and tailored to each state/country. In the UK it lists something like 500 specific laws you agree to not reference if you try and challenge. In the US it references standard NDA exceptions. What stays the same is this: you are never allowed to talk about facebook again in any situation where you opinion is either broadcast, recorded or written down. You may ask for permission first, but there is no expectation of facebook agreeing. They also want to be able to edit what is said. If you break that condition, then they will take you to court for all yeeting cash, plus damages and legal fees. In return they promise not to bad mouth you. However the maximum that they are willing to "indemnify" is $25. (or it might be $250) So when Wynn-Williams was smeared by facebook during the first legal fight, the most they are liable is $250. It also appears to not break the NDA, which is also interesting as its a clause that both facebook and the Yeetee agree to uphold. Which is fun because facebook is all about connecting people.

Wish I had this restraint. I’ve been vibing everything I can think of. Once deployed it becomes natural selection for which vibes live and which die. Solo vibey self hosting llm usage - bliss. Corporate agentic engineering working with others - soul crushing.

comments.author: jjcm
comments.text: In some ways it's better, in some ways it's worse. It's certainly easier than ever to spin up a VPS/cloudflare proxy and deploy. Agents can pretty much do that end to end. The bigger issue is you're then accountable for keeping up with security. Previously that meant using fail2ban and running a system update every few months. Now it means patching within 24hrs of a CVE9+ dropping, which is happening at an accelerated rate. It got so bad during October I made https://firefighter.sh/ as a joke (a root-permissioned agent that continuously monitors for CVEs and patches your system live as soon as they drop - it's a security nightmare given the nondeterministic aspect of AI), but I'm actually starting to come around to the idea for my non-critical servers.

comments.author: markhermeling
comments.text: Well written piece and certainly on-topic. There is a ton of conversation going on how AI can assist with formal methods. Personally I am having great success using Ada SPARK. The SPARK subset has been greatly enhanced over the past years. I spent yesterday taking existing C repos, translating to SPARK, lifting it to SPARK Silver (absence of runtime errors) and then reporting the findings to the various maintainers. All as a background activity. Result: integer overflows, typically on boundary conditions, some logic mistakes, again on boundary conditions. I have not looked into Magmide, but I think the next breakthrough is a combination of something like SysMLv2 to describe architecture and requirements, TLA+ for modeling and formal proofs at the system level and then Lean or SPARK for the implementation.

comments.author: ianjbutler
comments.text: Unification of programming languages and modeling languages is the holy grail of course, and it’s certainly no longer a pipe dream, but we suffer much from ignoring the easy wins in the middle ground. We could iteratively move towards this sort of thing by basically programming more directly with more formal stuff more often, basically thinking in terms of automata, process algebras, graph algorithms, etc. that’s the real design vocabulary now, not something like loops or objects For example.. abstractions from FSMs to kahn processes whatnot can all compile to Petri nets, and suddenly you can embed a formally checked subset of a classic and well understood control flow or dataflow or graph transforms, but using the idioms available in your language (decorators, templates, annotation). You write the formal model and the informal implementation side by side, using each to generate/elaborate/constrain the other. There’s only one whole but it has two distinct views, neither of which is complete or standing alone

comments.author: socketcluster
comments.text: We need secure, stable, modular components and platforms but I don't see how formal verification will help with this. The problem with formal verification is that it only lets you validate the solution against the spec, but it doesn't do anything in terms of validating the spec against reality. The spec can have a lot of conflicts. Also, as the complexity of the code grows, the contradictions and conflicts in the spec increase. A few weeks ago, Claude wrote me a short formal proof which proved that formal proofs cannot guarantee protection from software bugs or vulnerabilities in most realistic settings; especially when software requirements change too frequently. It made some assumptions about non-salvageability which I didn't ask for a proof for but it gave me some anecdotes from formally verified projects like SeL4 where letters from collaborators hinted that small changes to the code would sometimes require rewriting large parts of the proof. Unfortunately, we can't stop software from changing until we've developed platforms which provide optimal modularity. Optimally modular software has the property that code in dependencies (the leaves) has to be modified less frequently and less substantially than code of the dependents (the branches and trunk) in response to requirements changes. A useful measure may be the ratio of code changes dependent_code_delta/dependency_code_delta (over some period of time) where a high ratio is good and a low ratio is bad.

comments.author: spankalee
comments.text: Wow, I feel like Blaine is describe a language a lot like the one I'm working on now, Zena: https://zena-lang.dev/ I started Zena from wanting a TypeScript-like syntax that compiled to very efficient WebAssembly GC, and AssemblyScript had issues... The motivation for targeting Wasm was as a good sandboxing and orchestration unit for AI-generated code. So, out of both general PL curiosity and enthusiasm, and an attempt to make a language that's good for AI generation, I started adding what I thought were the best features from other languages with a lot of focus on correctness, structure, and optimizability: pattern matching with exhaustiveness checking, ADTs and sum types via sealed classes, value types, async cancelation / structured concurrency, ownership and borrow checking for resources, unicode safe strings, and recently I added runtime contracts and I'll start on refinement types and some kind of proof system soon. The idea is exactly to take a mainstream and familiar-looking language and add more cutting-edge and academic features that help with software correctness. I wrote about some of this here, though not the formal methods parts: https://zena-lang.dev/blog/2026/09/languages-for-the-ai-era/

comments.author: porcoda
comments.text: Dafny, SPARK Ada, Why3, Verus, Frama-C, TLA+, etc. are all sort of in this direction for different languages and styles of verification. It is nice to see them getting attention now that LLMs make them digestible for a broader set of programmers. I'm not sure one can start with a goal of creating a "mainstream" language that is verification-oriented. Mainstreamness comes from adoption. I'd look at those past languages (like the ones I listed), and ask "why did these not go mainstream" or "why did they not see broad adoption", and try some new ideas to address their gaps to see if a new one will catch on. But the "mainstream" part seems backwards as the goal - if it’s verifiable, ergonomic, flexible, and accessible, maybe it will go mainstream.

comments.author: pcstl
comments.text: Since it's what everyone is going to be worrying about: This result does not matter practically for cybersecurity. The best practical algorithm for solving elliptic curve DLP is BSGS (Baby Step, Giant Step) which grows as 2^{b/2+o(b)} in the key length. This result claims 2^O(b/(log log b)) which is technically subexponential, but since that `log log b` term grows so slowly it pretty much would only beat BSGS for absolutely gigantic keys.

comments.author: layer8
comments.text: A randomized subexponential-time algorithm for the discrete logarithm problem has been known for close to 50 years: https://pages.cs.wisc.edu/~cs812-1/adleman.pdf The present deterministic algorithm is highly unlikely to have practical consequences for cryptographic protocols in use.
